#### About Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz

Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz (1646–1716) was a German polymath—philosopher, mathematician, jurist, and diplomat—who developed calculus independently of Newton and a metaphysical system of monads. Serving courts at Mainz and Hanover, he corresponded across Europe’s republic of letters.

### Interpretation

Leibniz's phrase comes from the Theodicy and has been mocked more than read. His claim is not that this world contains no suffering but that among all worlds God could have created, this one has the greatest balance of metaphysical good — and that God's choice is guided by goodness, not arbitrary. The argument trades on the notion of compossibility: not everything good can exist together. Voltaire's Candide attacked the optimistic misuse of the idea rather than the argument itself.

#### Why it matters

The serious version raises a real question: if goods conflict and cannot all be realised, what does an optimal choice look like? Mockery does not dispose of it.

### Questions readers arrive with

#### What is the source of the quotation “the best of all possible worlds”?

“the best of all possible worlds” comes from Essais de Théodicée（1710）, attributed to Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz.

#### What does Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz mean by order?

Philosophers ask whether order is discovered in nature, imposed by rulers, or cultivated through custom. Chaos and creativity stand as its counterparts. This passage enters that discussion through order.
